title: The Ninth Bell
briefing:
Ezra Halloway, pawnbroker of Ashfen Row, was found dead behind his own counter on the morning of the fifteenth. The door was bolted from the inside. The constabulary have written apoplexy and gone home.

His sister-in-law does not believe it. She says he had been sleeping in the shop for a week, with every shutter nailed, and that he was frightened of something he would not name.

objectives.text: Establish how the room was sealed

clues.title: The door was bolted from within
clues.text: A heavy iron bolt, thrown across and still in its housing when the constables broke the frame. No trick of string could have thrown it from outside.

clues.title: The shutters were nailed shut
clues.text: Every window shuttered and nailed from the inside — and the nail heads are bright. This was done in the last week, not thirty years ago.

clues.title: No wound anywhere on him
clues.text: Not a mark. His face is fixed in an expression the undertaker has twice tried to smooth out.

clues.title: A watch stopped at four past nine
clues.text: A gentleman's pocket-watch lying open by his right hand, stopped at 9:04. It is not wound down — it has stopped.

clues.title: Two cups on the counter
clues.text: Two, not one. The second has a dried ring inside it and was set down in a hurry, off the saucer.

clues.title: Eleven days in another hand
clues.text: Thirty-one years of Halloway's careful copperplate, and then eleven days of entries written by somebody imitating it badly.

clues.title: Coal dust on the cellar stair
clues.text: Smudged on the treads — and the smears point upward. Somebody came up these stairs, they did not go down them.

clues.title: The coal chute is bolted too
clues.text: Bolted from the inside, like everything else in this building. The cellar has no other way out.

clues.title: The takings were never touched
clues.text: Nine pounds and change sitting in an unlocked-from-within strongbox. Whoever was here did not come for money.

clues.title: The watch is soaked through
clues.text: Spirituality clings to the case like grease. This is a sealed artefact, and it has been used — recently, and on someone who did not consent.

clues.title: His last minute was not his own
clues.text: The divination shows a memory replaying behind his eyes: a fire, a stairwell, a woman's name. None of it is his. He died inside somebody else's worst hour.

clues.title: Someone waited down here
clues.text: The impression of a person sitting very still, for hours, in the dark, listening to boots on the floor above.

clues.title: He was frightened for a week
clues.text: Ilsabet Crane: he had taken to sleeping in the shop, would not say why, and had begun asking her whether a thing could be given back to someone who never came for it.

clues.title: The shop was opened to a crowd
clues.text: Constable Rell forced the door at half past six. Nine or ten neighbours pushed in behind him before he could keep them out.

clues.title: The bell-pull sounded at nine
clues.text: The house opposite heard Halloway's shop bell at the ninth bell of St. Ferrin, and a raised voice after it — one voice, they thought, or perhaps two.

clues.title: Cass says he left at eight
clues.text: The apprentice: locked up at eight, crossed the Ash, slept at his mother's house in Barrow Fields, heard the news at noon.

clues.title: The last ferry is at seven
clues.text: Sil Mowbray, who works it: the last crossing to Barrow Fields is seven o'clock and there is no bridge for four miles. Nobody crossed the Ash at eight.

clues.title: The alibi cannot stand
clues.text: Put the ferry times to him and he stops talking altogether. He did not cross the river that night, because he could not have.

clues.title: A collector has been buying on the Row
clues.text: A gentleman calling himself Vane has spent three months buying queer clockwork off Ashfen Row, and paying more than queer clockwork is worth.

deductions.title: Nothing left this shop after it was shut
deductions.text: Door bolted, shutters nailed, chute bolted — every opening fastened from the inside. Whoever was in here when it was sealed was still in here.

deductions.title: He waited in the cellar and walked out with the crowd
deductions.text: The dust points up the stairs, someone sat in that dark for hours, and at half six a crowd of ten pushed into the shop. He did not need to leave a sealed room. He needed only to leave with everybody else.

deductions.title: The watch stopped his heart
deductions.text: No wound, a sealed artefact steeped in use, and a dead man drowning in a memory that belonged to somebody else. Wind that watch in front of a man and it will show him the worst hour of a stranger's life until his heart gives out.

deductions.title: He died at four minutes past nine
deductions.text: The bell, the raised voices, and a watch that stopped rather than ran down. The hour is fixed, and it is an hour when the apprentice claims to have been across a river.

deductions.title: Cass was selling the stock and forging the book
deductions.text: Eleven days of imitated copperplate, and a collector on the Row paying over the odds for exactly the sort of thing Halloway took in. The apprentice was selling his master's stock and writing the gaps closed.

deductions.title: Cass was in the shop that night
deductions.text: Two cups, one set down in a hurry, and an alibi that requires a ferry that had stopped running an hour before he says he took it.

deductions.title: Nobody came here for money
deductions.text: Nine pounds sitting untouched in the strongbox while a frightened man nailed his own shutters shut. Whatever was wanted in this shop, it was not the takings.

resolutions.label: Name Cass Whitlow, and hand the watch to the Club
resolutions.summary: The whole account: the forgery, the struggle, the artefact, and the cellar.
resolutions.epilogue:
You lay it out for Rell in the order he can write down: the ledger first, then the ferry, then the cellar. He does not ask how you knew to look in the cellar, which is a kindness, and you suspect a deliberate one.

Cass Whitlow confesses in the doorway of his mother's house, before anyone has finished asking. He says he only meant to take the watch. He says he did not know it would do that. Watching his face, you believe him, and it does not help.

The Star seals the watch in lead and lime and signs it into the Club's cupboard. The Hermit says nothing about your part in it at all, which from him is the loudest possible approval.

resolutions.label: Name Cass Whitlow, and say nothing of the watch
resolutions.summary: Enough to hang the boy. Not enough to explain what actually killed the man.
resolutions.epilogue:
Rell takes the sealed room and the broken alibi and is satisfied by both. He writes manslaughter, because a nineteen-year-old with no wound on the body is easier to file than the alternative.

What you do not give him is the watch. It goes back into the shop's stock, and the shop's stock goes to auction on the tenth, and somewhere in this city a stranger is going to wind it.

The Tower hears the account and looks at you for a while. 'You left a thing running,' he says, and goes back to watching the door.

resolutions.label: Give the Club the artefact and let the verdict stand
resolutions.summary: The dangerous thing is off the street. The boy walks.
resolutions.epilogue:
You hand the watch to the Star, who takes it in a cloth without touching it, and the constabulary's verdict of apoplexy goes into the record unchallenged.

It is the safe call. The thing that kills people is in a lead box, and no one had to be told that lead boxes are a category of object that exists.

Ilsabet Crane pays you anyway. She counts it out slowly and asks, at the end, whether you found out what he was frightened of. You tell her he was frightened of the wrong thing. It is true, and it is not an answer, and she knows the difference.

resolutions.label: Put it to Cass privately, and take his price for silence
resolutions.summary: You know enough to ruin him. He would rather pay.
resolutions.epilogue:
He pays out of the Vane money, in a doorway on Ashfen Row, and he is so relieved that he thanks you. That is the part you will keep.

You tell the widow her brother-in-law's heart gave out. She accepts it, because you are the professional and she is not, and she presses your hand at the door.

The Hermit does not ask what you concluded. He writes 'unresolved' in the Club's book in his slow careful hand, and lets you watch him do it.

resolutions.label: Tell her it was his heart, and take no fee
resolutions.summary: You have nothing worth the saying.
resolutions.epilogue:
You tell Ilsabet Crane what the constabulary told her, in better words, and refuse the fee because taking it would be the second unkindness.

She thanks you for your honesty. On the way out you pass the shop, which is shuttered again, and the shutters are somebody else's problem now.

The Club's book gets one line. The Hermit writes it without looking up.

leads.label: Ask along the wharf about the river timetable
leads.description: Somebody on the Ash works every crossing there is. One of them will remember a fare, and all of them will remember the hours.
leads.successText: Three hands tell you the same thing without conferring, which is how you know it is the timetable and not an opinion: last crossing at seven, no bridge for four miles, and a great deal of grumbling about both.
leads.failureText: You buy two rounds and learn a good deal about a dispute over mooring fees. Nobody wants to talk about hours to a stranger who is obviously asking about hours.

leads.label: Pay somebody to name the collector
leads.description: There is always a man who knows which gentleman has been overpaying, and he is always more expensive than he looks.
leads.successText: The name comes back the same from two directions: Vane. Three months on the Row, buying clockwork that does not tell time, paying in the Alley, never haggling.
leads.failureText: Your money buys a name that turns out to belong to a corn factor in Barrow Fields who has been dead since spring.

leads.label: Sit on the shop from the coffee house opposite
leads.description: A night in a window seat with a cold cup, watching who comes back to a house where a man died.
leads.successText: Nobody comes back. But you get the neighbours' evening in order, and the house opposite is very clear: the shop bell went at the ninth bell of St. Ferrin, and a voice went up after it.
leads.failureText: You sit until three in the morning and learn that the coffee house waters its coffee. Nobody comes, nothing happens, and the day is gone.

leads.label: Read the parish and pledge records
leads.description: Thirty-one years of a pawnbroker's filings are a matter of public record if you know which clerk to be pleasant to.
leads.successText: The shop's quarterly returns are in Halloway's hand for thirty-one years and in somebody else's for the last eleven days — the same somebody who has been imitating it badly in the ledger on the counter.
leads.failureText: Four hours of a clerk's opinions and a great deal of dust. The relevant volume is out for rebinding and will be back on the twentieth.

leads.label: Read up on sealed timepieces
leads.description: The Club's shelves have four books on artefacts that hold an hour. Three of them are wrong, and knowing which is the trick.
leads.successText: You find it in the fourth book, in a footnote, in a language the author clearly did not expect to be checked: a class of sealed timepiece that replays a borrowed hour to whoever winds it. The description matches the thing in your pocket exactly.
leads.failureText: You read for a day and come away with three contradictory taxonomies and a headache. The books on this subject were written by people who did not want to be understood.
